utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. [French on English channel]. Is French now on the fourth channel?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I also received a French translation on channel number 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, let's start all over again. Hopefully English will come back. Good morning once again, and welcome to everybody. May we please have the appearances. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Alan Tieger, Laurie Sartorio, and case manager, Donnica Henry Frijlink for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Microphone, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge. Good morning, Your Honour. Gregory Kehoe and Luka Misetic for General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Cedo Prodanovic, Jadranka Slokovic, and Tihomir Mak, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Miroslav Separovic representing for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Separovic. You are alone today. The last Status Conference was held on the 9th of February, 2007. Pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Status Conference shall be convened within 120 days of the last in order to organise exchanges between the parties to ensure the expeditious preparation for trial and to allow the accused to raise issues in relation to the case. On the 2nd of April a 65 ter Conference was held in preparation for the present conference. Before we carry on, may I just find out, I notice that we've got only General Gotovina in the courtroom. I gather the other accused are excused. There is no videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General Gotovina, do you have any -- can you hear me, first of all, and understand me in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And how are you? How is your health, General Gotovina? THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for asking. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any issue you would like to raise in relation to the Detention Unit? THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] My Defence will represent me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. The next issue that I would like us to deal with is -- relates to conflict of interest and trial scheduling. A decision of the conflict of interest, if not already issued by the time of this Status Conference will be rendered shortly. That is relating to Mr. Prodanovic and Ms. Slokovic. And of course resulting from that decision and the decision on the position of Mr. Separovic, scheduling would have to be addressed in due course. I guess it is -- must be clear this time to everybody that it is almost impossible to start by the 7th of May. That being so, however, we should not think that the scheduling should be -- will be pushed back for far too long. I think we need to go over the problems of representation and the questions of appeal. I know that an appeal has been lodged by the by -- Mr. Markac's counsel. And make sure that all those things are done as soon as possible so that we can reschedule the case. Are there any comments that any of counsel would like to make on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure there will be more substantive and detailed comments in due course as we grapple with this issue. On behalf of the Prosecution we appreciate the fact that the Court has raised it so forthrightly. We think it does need to be addressed substantively so we can make appropriate arrangements and as we begin to discuss that we will be happy to contribute accordingly, but in the abstract I have no further comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Indeed it is still in the abstract at this stage that I don't expect much comment, but just in case anybody has got anything to say. Mr. Misetic, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That being the case, maybe we can then pass on to the next point. Agreed facts. At the last conference the parties stated that while they had met to discuss agreed facts little progress had been made due to their perception that the schedule was accelerated. And in the Prosecution's submission pursuant to Rule 65 ter it stated at paragraph 6, "Given the scheduled start of trial in early May, 2007, the Prosecution notes that no admission has yet been made by the Defence nor any agreement been reached with respect to non-contested facts or law. As a result, the Prosecution assumes for now that all issues of fact and law are contested at this time. This being said, the Prosecution will continue to attempt to reach agreement with the various Defence teams with respect to agreed facts or law to the extent possible, and notes that efforts to reach agreement on issues such as exhumations and prosecutions of crimes are underway." Is that still the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Probably important to note that that recitation of the state of affairs was not intended in any way, and I hope was not interpreted as any kind of finger pointing at my learned friends, simply that -- and a summary of what the parties agreed was the -- the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, decisions have now been issued on the question of jurisdiction, form of indictment, and under Rule 73 bis (D), and the outer limits of the case ought to be clear at least, and the parties ought to be able to discuss agreed facts in a more conclusive manner, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this matter was discussed to some extent at the 65 ter Conference yesterday. We certainly agree with the Court that the evolving circumstances surrounding some aspects of the indictment have produced a situation which renders the possibility of identifying the areas of potential agreement more likely. That -- now, setting aside, for the moment, the -- the question of the outstanding interlocutory appeal on jurisdiction, which is another matter, the problem raised by the parties was not so much the uncertainties surrounding the issues that might be discussed, but simply the opportunity to do so. And I think that was a matter raised before the Bench on earlier occasions. It was reiterated yesterday. The focus was on the logistics of the process, which do require a dedicated period of time to reach fruition. I think all the parties attempted yesterday to explain in somewhat greater detail the stages involved in that process and therefore the requirements of time. That has been the issue. As the Court just noted we may face a situation now or may find ourselves in a situation now that is more propitious for dedicating certain periods of time for this specific purpose. And if so, the parties have indicated their willingness to engage in the process and we will certainly do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Any view on that point in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have to echo some of the responses that -- comments that Mr. Tieger made with regard to time. Now that we do have some period of time, we will of course dedicate our efforts to coming to some agreed facts or a large portion of those facts, I do believe. Keeping in mind, Judge, that by Thursday, I do believe it's Thursday we are scheduled to file our pre-trial brief as well, so we will have the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution and, of course, the Defence will have theirs. And I think that we will be able to use both of those documents as a starting point for many of these agreed facts moving, of course, from the larger facts to the smaller. But I do believe that with this period of time we can dedicate ourselves to that. I do once again want to footnote what Mr. Tieger noted with regard to the indictment itself, there has been an appeal filed on the Rule 72 decisions on jurisdiction that the Trial Chamber has made, just so Your Honour knows that has, in fact, been filed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no, I understand Judge, but I was just talking about from the standpoint Your Honour said there have been decisions on that, that is outstanding. But that is not going to prevent discussions on agreed facts. There are a significant number of agreed facts that we can come to a concrete resolution on with a period of time. And I think counsel will all agree would that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prodanovic. I don't want to repeat what has already been said. I simply want to say that when the trial was scheduled for the 7th of May, it was not possible to expect that we would have any time to talk about the agreed facts. Now that the trial has been delayed for a certain period of time, I think we will be able to start this process and we are eager to part in it. Of course we expect initiative on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prodanovic. Any comments, Mr. Separovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I agree fully with my colleague, Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I make a proposal perhaps, also that there are efforts on reaching agreement on facts, should try to also cover, amongst others, facts and crime-base evidence, including evidence on the accuseds' various positions, victims, lists, and identity of victims and the exhumation evidence, as indeed you are already trying to do and also the applicable law. If there isn't anything else, I would like us to then deal with the next item on the agenda, which is the comprehensive motions under Rules 92 bis, 92 ter, and for protective measures. At the last 65 ter Conference and Status Conference, the Prosecution was asked when it would be in a position to submit comprehensive motions under these rules. The Prosecution replied that it would submit such motions between the submission of its 65 ter submission and the 65 ter submission of the Defence. If this has not been done before this Status Conference, in light of the dead-line of the 5th of April for the 65 ter Defence submission, the Prosecution is being reminded to submit such motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution did submit a motion on March 27th, as requested, or ordered. I understand from the legal officer that the Court was interested -- let me step back for a moment. And that motion outlined a number of protective measures of -- a broader form of protective measures was requested with respect to 92 bis and 92 quater and 92 ter, it outlined some of the steps that the Prosecution anticipated taking with respect to certain witnesses. I understand from the senior legal officer that the Bench would like formal motions upon which the Court would rule as soon as possible. And we discussed that at the conference yesterday. My suggestions would be, and noting that the March 27th motion indicated that the Prosecution anticipating filing approximately 14 motions under 92 bis and/or 92 quater, that we identify a date now by which I'll propose a date, the Prosecution would submit at least a certain number of motions for the court to rule on. Specifically with respect to these measures, I think the legal officer referred to them as bundled submissions and I understood that to mean the concrete motions upon which the Court could rule, upon which my learned colleagues could respond. Now, part of the reason that those weren't submitted is that for the reasons described in the motion the Prosecution needed additional time to actually directly contact witnesses, and that's -- we're in the process of doing that. But I would say irrespective of the -- of whether or not that process has been completed, we would suggest filing these -- or at least a number of these concrete motions for 92 bis or 92 quater but I think, if I understood the senior legal officer correctly and if I gauge the Court's intention to move the process forward, at least incrementally insofar as possible, that that would be the step the Court would be looking for, and we can do that with respect to the particular witnesses, particular testimonies, that have been identified even in light of the particular logistical difficulties. So we can file X number of motions by the week of April 16th, and indicate to the Court at the same time whether we anticipate additional motions to follow. Now, with respect to 92 bis, that will involve liaising with the Registry because additional missions will be necessary, both in Serbia and in Croatia, to obtain the statements via the Registry upon which certain of motions will be based. But to the extent possible, we can get other motions that have been brought to a stage where they can be submitted to the Court, before the Court, during that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to guesstimate what percentage of the 14 motions that are anticipated X amount will be? The majority of them or just a few?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I would say -- and I misspoke slightly, I think there are about 20 motions anticipated under Rule 92 bis and Rule 92 quater and I think we could have more than half submitted by that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think any of the counsel would like to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just to the extent that, and this did come up yesterday at the 65 ter Conference, and to the extent that some of these witnesses who have given statements have said they would like some protective measures. I just would inform the Court we will resist some of those and we will respond. Some of them we will not, of course, but there will be some discussion, but we're also waiting to see what the list is of who these witnesses are. If it is any indication of some of the more professional witnesses who have asked for protective measures, we would of course resist that, but we will wait until the appropriate time to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Kehoe, we agree. We understand that it is in the interests of the proper administration of justice for trials to be in public, and to that extent we understand that you always have that right to resist. Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Prodanovic, do you have anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is the appropriate moment to touch upon the way that the witnesses are going to be examined as part of the protective measures, then I would have something to say. I am working according to yesterday's agenda, for yesterday's conference, and it's on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's hear what you have to say on the point then, Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The request of the Prosecution to limit the disclosure of the identity of three witnesses to the Defence, I have to say the following: As far as Witness P-15 is concerned, we have completely contrary position. We think that there are no factors that could allow the withdrawal of the -- his identity to the Defence. P-16, not P-15. It's a witness to the events, member of Croatian army. And if we are to cross-examine him and his credibility, we absolutely have to know his identity. You have to bear in mind that there are no extraordinary circumstances which would normally warrant the procedure in which the Defence would not be allowed to know his identity. I would like to reference you to the Tadic decision in this relation, and the extraordinary situation which would be required here does not exist anymore in Republic of Croatia. And since the situation has been changed for better, I also have to say that it's precisely the reason why Ademi and Norac case has been referred to Croatia. I don't think that it is possible to just generally talk about danger for this witness, and especially not the situation in which this danger would be produced simply by Defence knowing his identity. Therefore we are certainly going to submit a separate motion and are going to resist this request and require his identity to be divulged to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It is always your right to do so. I'm not quite sure whether you are really on the Prosecution witness list or are you still on the 92 bis and 92 ter things. Or am I behind?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the problem is that we don't have an agenda for today, so I'm referring to yesterday's agenda. Agenda for 65 ter Conference. There we also spoke about the Prosecution witnesses and their list, and some of them were supposed to have their identities protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just then apologise for the fact that you don't have an agenda. I thought you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be then slightly ahead of the agenda, then maybe we should simply leave it for the next point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's do that. Maybe we can deal with it under that heading. Mr. Separovic, any comments on the point at issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I also wanted to say something about protective measures, but nothing for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Separovic. That then disposes of that item on comprehensive motions under Rules 92 bis and 92 ter. And the next item now then becomes the Prosecution's witness list, and I think this is where Mr. Prodanovic was trying to lead us, but before we ask him to talk again, anything from the Prosecution? I notice that the -- yes, in -- the Prosecution noted in its motion of the 27th of March that witnesses number 64 and 158 through to 162 should be removed from the Prosecution witness list for the reasons stated in the motion for temporary protective measures. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have the numbers in front of me, but I believe that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. And that number 64 has decided not to testify as a result of threats. The other five are the same as Witnesses P-1 to P-5 and are inadvertently mentioned twice in the list as numbers 158 to 162.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not aware that there's any confusion among the parties with respect to those submissions and the witnesses who are now -- who remain on the witness list. If -- if the Court or my learned friends have any questions, we will be, of course, happy to clarify. But as far as I'm aware, the submissions were clear enough to them, and I think the -- my recollection is that the adjustments were fairly straightforward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, Judge. And to the extent there has been really any confusion on this, I think we have been working together to try and resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Prodanovic could also confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prodanovic. Can we then deal with disclosure between the parties. At the last Status Conference the Prosecution stated that it would inform the SLO on -- by which date it would be able to conclude disclosure. As far as I know, no such information has been given or received from the Prosecution, and are there any outstanding issues that need to be dealt with under disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me indicate to the Court part of the discussion that took place at the 65 ter yesterday, and part of the follow-up that resulted. With under disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me indicate to the Court part of the discussion that took place at the 65 ter yesterday, and part of the follow-up that resulted. First of all by way of back-drop, it may be helpful because I may be alluding to some of these factors in the course of explaining to the Bench where we now stand. Some of the measures that were taken by the Prosecution during the course of disclosure of the 65 ter materials. In discussions with the Defence, it would helpful for them to disclose in a fairly unusual way, but one that was deemed quite helpful by the parties. That included providing the disclosures on a hard drive to -- three separate hard drives to each Defence teams and also creating a hyper-linked exhibit list which would facilitate the process of identifying the particular exhibits. And the hard drives were provided, the hyper-linked exhibit list is being completed. I should also mention that throughout the course of this process, and something that Mr. Kehoe alluded to a few moments ago, the exchange of information and level of cooperation between the Prosecution and the Defence, I think, has been extremely high and extremely gratifying to all parties. Yesterday we received, just before the 65 ter Conference, a list from Mr. Misetic from Mr. Gotovina's Defence, and then at the 65 ter Conference a list from Mr. Separovic on behalf of General Markac of documents and or/statements that they had been unable to locate and needed some help in finding. If I remember correctly, Mr. Separovic indicated that he was missing some 40 statements or so and approximately 150 documents. Mr. Misetic's list, I think, encompassed about 150 documents or so. The particular numbers aren't so important in light of what I'm going to say, but that's the general situation that prevailed yesterday. Thanks to some extraordinary efforts by Ms. Henry-Frijlink between the course of yesterday and late last night, we went over those materials. What I can tell the Court is the following: First of all with respect to the statements that Mr. Separovic alluded to, we determined that those had been previously sent to him in March via e-mail. And I'll provide him with the exact times of those e-mails and so that he can readily identify those. In addition, and perhaps more importantly, we went over systematically, or I should say Ms. Henry Frijlink link went over systematically, the list. And we are providing to the Defence today, virtually every document contained on the list. For the most part those were, it turned out to be, in fact, documents that we are confident had been disclosed and were contained on the hard drive, but for matters of convenience we decided it was easier simply to reburn them on a CD and provide them to the Defence today and that's what we intend to do. That CD has been burned and we can provide it after the Status Conference. In addition, there were a small fraction of documents that we believe were not on the hard drive because they were inadvertently omitted from the exhibit list, although referenced in the pre-trial brief. And we provide those today by way of supplementing the exhibit list. They will also be contained on the CD. Finally, we noted that a certain number, and again a relatively small number of statements were still pending translation. I double-checked on that. I am advised that the translation authorities believe that can be completed by the end of this week, and I reconfirmed that this morning. So even if there's some slippage in that projected dead-line, those statements will be available, translations of those statements will be available in very short order. So that essentially is the state of play at the moment. And it was, of course, helpful that we were all face to face and were provided with specific references that we could double-check and respond to in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you are on your feet, before you sit down, can you address the Rule 70 disclosures?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I've neglected to mention that and I'm glad you've raised that. The -- we are running through that once more, particularly in light of the fact that one of the principal providers on Friday cleared a significant number of documents. So we want to run through the entire Rule 70 pending matters to ensure insofar as possible, that first of all, all of those that have been cleared are now made available to the Defence to determine which have not been cleared and recontact the providers forthwith to urge them to accelerate the process of responding to our request for clearances. But my current understanding is that in the wake of the recent clearance the -- the bulk of those pending Rule 70 matters will have been cleared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand you quite clearly. When you say they have been cleared and the bulk of those pending matters will have been cleared, are you able to give us a time-line by which a disclosure might take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of the documents that are cleared? Within one week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any comments from -- yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to confirm what Mr. Tieger had said; however, I wanted to point out for the Trial Chamber the circumstances from the view of the Defence in light of the fact that a pre-trial brief is due Thursday. At the time of the filing of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, there were anywhere between 35 and 50 witness statements cited in the brief that we did not have possession of. We have been working with the Prosecution to resolve that issue. There was an e-mail sent shortly thereafter, I think maybe the Monday after the brief was filed Friday, where we did receive those statements. With respect to the documents cited in the pre-trial brief, there were around 150 documents cited in the brief; it's probably half of them. The documents are the B/C/S and English translations of the same document, so we're talking roughly the neighbourhood of 50 to 75 documents cited in the brief that we did not have access to until either last week when I received a copy of the hard drive or today when we received a copy of the CD. In light of the fact our pre-trial brief is due Thursday and we're still receiving material from the Prosecution in terms of documents that are actually cited in their brief, I wanted to alert the Court that we are working feverishly to meet the Court's dead-line of filing the pre-trial brief; however, I wanted to advise you that to the extent there are any issues that we need to address that are cited in documents that we are now receiving from the Prosecution, it may be that we'll have to alert the Court to a problem and ask for a short extension, but that is not our plan right now, and we intend to file the brief on time on Thursday, but I wanted to inform the Court of our situation right now. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Misetic. If that eventuality does arise, is it not possible to file your brief to the extent that you have information and reserve the right to supplement it later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour; if that is the Court's preferred manner of proceeding, that's fine. I do want to indicate that it is our intention, even though we're here in The Hague right now, to meet the dead-line on Thursday, and if for some reason, we feel that there is an issue raised in one of the documents we have just received, with the Court's indulgence we may just file the brief with a note that says we would like to address the issue at a later date or invite the Court to invite us to file a written submission on that issue, should the Court want us to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you did ask for a postponement, how long -- if you wanted to file a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Over the weekend so we could file it on Monday or Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, then, yeah. Thank you. Mr. Prodanovic. Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We basically join the proposal put forward by the Defence of General Gotovina. We would also like to see these additional witness statements that have not been disclosed to us until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's understandable, Mr. Prodanovic. Thank you very much. Mr. Separovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also agree. I gave a list to my learned friends from the Prosecution yesterday with the documents that are missing. I was glad to hear that Mr. Tieger was able to find some of them, but I have to tell you that there are 45 witness statements, interviews, that are missing. I am not saying that we did not receive summaries. We received the summaries. But we cannot find 45 witness statements. They are still outstanding. We are unable to access documents. We simply do not have them. I hope that this problem has been resolved and if it is case, I am very grateful to Mr. Tieger and we will not be raising these issues in the future if this has been resolved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Separovic. Mr. Tieger's very eager to answer to that. He stands up while you are still talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I don't want to make a problem where one doesn't exist. I think it is largely resolved. However, it is important not to confuse two things. Number one, documents that were disclosed but that the Defence was unable to locate for whatever reason, that -- those do represent the bulk of the documents we're talking about. And secondly, not to confuse pending translations of statements that were disclosed for the absence of any disclosure of statements. But with that clarification, I think we now find ourselves in a situation where everyone can proceed apace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if I might just ask a question. Is the Prosecution in a position to produce proof to the Defence, whenever they are queried, of delivery of certain documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in the -- we have generally engaged in the practice of responding to their notification of difficulties, and as I say, it has been helpful in particular that they have noted certain documents. We do so by specifically noting when those documents were disclosed and where they can be found. Having said that, it's struck us as much more expeditious to simply provide those documents again, so that we don't have to engage in the entire process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But we have attempted to do that at each juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand the question of difficulties. But then side by side that question, there is also the question of obligations. You are obliged to give certain disclosures, at times certain disclosures are supposed to be made within a certain time line, and, yes, you may have given them, they may have misplaced then, and they may then run into the difficulty they are not able to be access them, and they come back to you, and fine, I will give you another set. However, I want to know, for purposes of the Chamber, whether you are able to give proof when you have delivered because I would not want the time of the Court to be squandered because I have lost my papers and for three months I have not done anything, and in three months' time Mr. Tieger, out of the goodness of his heart gives me second copies, but he really is not obliged and I'm the one who is supposed to be on terms because I've lost my papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour. Number one, yes, we not only can demonstrate that those documents have been disclosed, but we attempt to do so when advised of the problem and have attempted to do so in various spread sheets. Number two, in fairness to my learned friends, I don't think -- I'm not sure it's a matter of misplacing the papers or the documents. There are -- there are access difficulties with some of the -- I'm advised by them, with some of the disclosure - what shall I call them? - machinery that they've brought our attention to. That's one of the reasons we provided the hard drive and the hyper-linked exhibit list, to try to obviate any such problems. But at the same time, I don't want it misunderstood that the Prosecution hasn't attempted each time it has redisclosed, to also indicate when and how the previous disclosure was made. So there is no -- certainly no finger pointing on anyone's part, but I don't want the Court to understand that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I understand -- I understand that there's there no finger-pointing. However, when I came on this case from the 5th of December last year, particularly on this question of disclosure, there has not been any modicum of agreement, there has always been -- no, no, the Prosecution claims very few documents are outstanding. The Defence claims lots and lots of documents are outstanding. And we've got to come to a time when we should be able to say: Prosecution, show that you have disclosed you have that you had to disclose. Defence, do you have that, and if you don't have it, you can't blame the Prosecution. You can ask the Prosecution to redisclose because -- for whatever reason you are not accessing your information. But you can't blame them. You can ask for indulgence. We've got to get to a time when we are able to put the blame where it belongs. At this -- for now, we have not done so. And I'm not intending to do so in the very near future, but there is going to come a time when the buck must stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think everyone understands that, Your Honour, and I appreciate the Court's comments. I believe that's what the parties have been attempting to do and especially in the face of the size of a case like this, so we make disclosures of a large volume of material. The Defence has gone through those disclosures. I think Mr. Misetic in particular has attempted to go through them for the most part as comprehensively as he could. He has then identified for us problems that exist. In fairness to both sides, I think, the percentage of problems, given the volume of material are relatively small and relatively predictable. Our response to the identification of any problems has been as proactive, and I think constructive as possible, that is to address them directly. So I think the parties have been attempting to proceed in precisely the spirit encouraged by the Court so that as quickly as possible everyone can be satisfied that that, what was intended to be disclosed, was received and is available, and to any extent it is not, it is immediately addressed so that we can narrow any gaps that exist. Today should be one example. The Defence specifically identified a number of documents that they could not locate from the recent 65 ter disclosures. We believe we've now responded comprehensively, I should say, except for as I understand it two documents which we we're still exporting from the system, but that it will be provided. Again, if there is any problem in that, I'm confident that we will be advised, but clearly the problems within that much narrower range of identified documents will be even smaller and we can quickly move to resolves that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your kindness is appreciated. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to follow up on what Mr. Tieger said and I want it to be clear from the Defence side as well. First, there is not an issue here where -- of good faith. I think all the parties are proceeding in good faith. The issue for us, and the reason I brought it up, was simply: All we care about is getting the documents, obviously. Either there has been a problem in terms of your review of the last four months since you've been in this case. I think the problem has been twofold. It's either been a situation where there are some documents that haven't been disclosed or, from our end, we've been having trouble finding documents that have been disclosed in light of the means of disclosure. In other words, there is an EDS system and other means of disclosure, that there have been problems in the electronic phase of trying to gain access to them. I think both sides are working in a spirit of, first, cooperation, and second, trying to move as expeditiously as possible to resolve those issues. So this is not for the purpose of laying blame, from their side and us or vice versa, but to keep the Court fully informed. The reason I bring it to your attention to was, regardless of those types of issues of why we don't have the documents. When the pre-trial brief was filed we didn't have them and in light of that, I wanted to keep you informed of what we didn't have, the scope of those the documents that we didn't have, as well as the fact that we are moving diligently to get our brief filed on Thursday. And in light of 50 witness statements and 150 or so documents, we're moving as fast as possible to get it filed but there may be a need for extension of a few days. I appreciate the Court's concern that there be a date where we can say all disclosure has been made. I think we are moving towards that date, and as long as we keep moving that way and they respond diligently to my requests, which I can tell the Court that they do, I think that date will probably arrive very shortly. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Do you have any contribution, Mr. Prodanovic? Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Separovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Separovic. Now, I think then we can close that point on that note, and move on to the next item, which is the pending motions and other pending matters. Now, on the 26th of March, 2007, the Gotovina Defence filed a motion pursuant to Rule 73, requesting Pre-Trial Chamber to strike parts of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, constituting affective amendment of the joinder indictment. On the 27th of March, 2007, the Prosecution filed the Prosecution's submission regarding manner of testimony for Prosecution witnesses, and on the same date the Prosecution filed a Prosecution motion for temporary protective measures. Now, with respect to the 27th March motions, Mr. Tieger, what the Chamber would like to confirm with you is whether those motions cover the Prosecution's request for an order of non-disclosure which was included in paragraph 13 of the Rule 65 ter submission of the 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The effective answer is yes, Your Honour, in the sense that we're not seeking specific relief by way of paragraph 13, which was more of a admonitory note out of an abundance of caution, but the 27th March motion is the operative document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the operative document. Thank you very much. Then on the 28th of March the Prosecution submitted its clarifications of the indictment following the decision on the form of the indictment. And following the authorisation by the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution will submit the clarification concerning the pleading of JCE by the 5th of April. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. On the 30th of March the Markac Defence made a submission pursuant to the Trial Chamber's 6th March decision on finding of misconduct of Mr. Separovic, which had ordered the Defence immediately to engage new counsel, and that new counsel was to inform the Trial Chamber by 30th of March of how much time would be needed to fully take over the case. Now, the Markac Defence submits that more time is needed to find replacement counsel and therefore requests an extension of time. The Defence also requests that trial start be delayed until the autumn of 2007, and I think we've touched on that at the beginning of this Status Conference this morning. And lastly -- and lastly, let me just mention that the parties -- or rather the 6th of March decision had requested the parties to inform the Court on how they thought the matter could be taken forward. Dealing with the Markac submission, let me just indicate once again, Mr. Separovic, that given the fact that your Defence team has noted an appeal, the appeal is pending, the fact that a decision in the Prodanovic, Slokovic matter is still outstanding, there is this uncertainty about the start time, so that there is an effective extra time that the Separovic defence is getting as a result of these developments. The Bench is unable to say at this stage by how long this effective postponement will be. It depends on how soon we get to resolve difficulties that we are facing. But I would therefore encourage you, and your client, to please move as expeditiously as you possibly can to resolve the problems from your side so that as and when the rest of the issues are resolved we are able to start the trial, or very near starting the trial. This may not necessarily be a reasoned-out answer to the issues you raise in your motions, but for the time being this is just a thinking that I am -- is going on in my mind and which I thought I should share with the parties, pending a comprehensive response to all these motions. Okay. Is there anybody who would like to say anything on these issues that I have just raised? Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Simply to note, Your Honour, that of course the concern from the Prosecution side, at least in part, is the scheduling of witnesses, many of whom we've now been in touch with. The -- and I appreciate the situation the Court finds itself in now, but at some point we'll -- we'll benefit from a date certain, or at least some indication that we can give our witnesses by way of planning, many of whom are located overseas, many of whom have busy schedules and need to adjust those schedules in order to make an appearance here. So that's a -- clearly a concern on our part. For the time being, obviously, we'll have them stand down. But as soon as the -- well, two things are clear. As soon as we can -- the sooner we can get some kind of date certain, understanding the uncertainties of the moment, the better. And in addition, we'll need sufficient lead time, and that generally involves six to eight weeks at a minimum to be able to go through the logistical process of going through VWS and so on, to schedule witnesses appropriately. In the meantime, we'll alert them to the uncertainties, try to project as accurately as we can, but that clearly involves difficulties for everyone. And those are among the factors we have to take into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Certainly. Let me just say this to all the parties, that certainly the Court will try, to its best, to accommodate the parties and give them sufficient lead time when once everything is certain. The only problem is that as of now everything -- nothing is certain. I don't know when the appeal is going to be heard and when the judgement will be handed down. A decision is still outstanding in the Prodanovic matter. I don't know how long it will take -- I don't know what the decision of the Appeals Chamber is going to be, I don't know what the Prodanovic team is going to do with the decision that is going to come down and what effect it's going to have. But let me just say that that decision will be handed down fairly soon. So nothing can be planned, even from the side of the Bench, in terms of thinking of dates and time lines, because we just don't know from what date do we start, when we start talking of time lines. But when all that information has been ascertained, the Chamber will take into account the logistical problems that all the parties are faced with. Okay? Having said that, is there any further comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nothing from General Gotovina, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few words, Your Honour. Regardless of the outcome of the appeal that I have instituted, in view of your request we are very actively seeking new counsel. We provided evidence to the effect that we haven't been able to engage one until now, but that doesn't mean that we will cease our efforts in that regard. Regardless of the outcome of the appeal, the decision as it stands now is not good for General Markac. It's not good for me either, but it's not my interests that we are concerned with right now. All I can tell you is that we are working on the problem. I will continue doing my best to contribute to the resolution of this problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for those words, Mr. Separovic. And that's also the motive of the Bench in sharing what I shared with you a few minutes ago about -- when I dealt with the motions filed for the Markac Chamber -- the Markac Defence team. I note that one of the things that you asked for was an extension of time. As I said to you, you have an effective extension of time; how long it will be, I really don't know. That I said because I realised that you are finding difficulty in finding replacement counsel in the region, and I just wanted to give you the comfort that there is some more time for you to carry on doing that, because it is also in the interests of the Chamber that you get this counsel as soon as possible so that, depending on the outcome of the appeal, that counsel should be -- should find sufficient time to update themselves on the trial. So, yes, we share the same concerns. Thank you very much. That brings me to the end of agenda, as I had it. Are there any issues that any of the parties would like to raise that are -- probably were not an the agenda. Let's start with you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No particular issue, Your Honour. I just wonder if the Court was going to specifically vacate the pre-trial date and the trial date, and then maybe have a Status Conference for sometime, an appropriate time thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe you could guide us on that one. I haven't had experience of that. When you want me to vacate, do I do that by order? Or can I do it right here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the Court can do it -- Mr. Kehoe seems to have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you can do anything you want, Judge. That's one of the beauties of wearing a red robe, Judge. I think you can just do it orally, Judge, and that would be fine. I don't think there's any need for anything other than an oral statement by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the scheduling order is then so vacated without any date certain. Was that all you wanted to raise, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's all I had, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Misetic, Mr. Kehoe, anything from the Gotovina team?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, from General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Separovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither do we, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then, there being no further business to do, that brings us to the end of the Status Conference, and the court stands adjourned.
